card.title: Riverbank Dwellers Moved Late and Three Workers Killed on the Ganga Clean-up
card.place: The Patna riverfront development on the Ganga, including Bhairwa Ghat and the Digha sewage treatment plant site, and the Beur and Begusarai works, Bihar, India

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA and IBRD)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-49550 of US$199 million and loan IBRD-80650 of US$801 million for the National Ganga River Basin Project (P119085), approved 31 May 2011 and effective 18 August 2011. The IBRD loan was cut to US$334,825,259 and US$514,233,533 was disbursed in all against the original US$1 billion commitment. Original closing was 31 December 2019 and actual closing 30 December 2021. Total project cost fell from US$1.556 billion to US$673,583,533. Environmental category A, full assessment. The implementing agency was the National Mission for Clean Ganga in the Ministry of Jal Shakti. The project's Environment and Social Management Framework was revised to include the provisions of India's Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013. Safeguards performance at closing was rated Moderately Satisfactory. The completion report of 28 February 2023 rated outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation quality Substantial; the Independent Evaluation Group's review agreed on all three (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 February 2023; IEG ICR Review, Bank document date 29 June 2023).

companies.name: National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG)
companies.role: The mission under the Department of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation in India's Ministry of Jal Shakti that implemented the project, working through state programme management groups. The completion report records that the programme management groups had dedicated systems for safeguards implementation, and that procurement capacity at state level and at the Central Pollution Control Board remained low (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 February 2023).
companies.desc: An Indian government body: a society registered under the Societies Registration Act 1860 which the River Ganga (Rejuvenation, Protection and Management) Authorities Order of 10 July 2016 also makes an authority under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986. The Order makes it the nodal agency for implementing the Order nationwide, requires it to prepare the Ganga basin management plan and to notify ecological flows, and lets it issue directions to state and district Ganga committees and local authorities. Its Director General is appointed by the central government at the rank of Additional Secretary or Secretary, and its accounts are audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General.

card.community: The project financed sewage treatment plants, sewer networks and a riverfront development to cut pollution going into the Ganga. Most investments used land already under existing treatment plants or government land transferred after a no-objection certificate, and where private land was needed the project bought it directly; the completion report records that direct purchase was dogged by prolonged price negotiations, contested ownership rights and complications in paying the final amounts. The only investment that required full land acquisition was the Patna riverfront development, which affected 249 families. Those affected were encroachers living in shacks and mud houses on the riverbank. Because compensation against the existing value of their assets and income would have been negligible, a flat rate of INR 150,000 and land for a house were agreed instead. The land allotment was then stalled for two years, and in the end extra cash was given instead of land. The completion report records a further complication: the sites were handed over to the contractor before the affected people had been resettled and before compensation was paid. The affected people were tracked down and compensated, and the report says this affected implementation of the investment, especially at Bhairwa Ghat. Beyond the riverfront, 20 households were affected by partial land acquisition and 234 households by economic losses. At closing all resettlement action plans had been fully implemented and one abbreviated plan was still open, to compensate three affected people at the Digha sewage treatment plant site. All the riverfront families were eventually compensated and given training to restore their incomes. In 2021 two fatal incidents at project sites in Bihar killed three labourers, one at Begusarai in March and two at Beur in May. The completion report's annex on the project's history states that the root-cause analysis indicated the accidents occurred through negligence on occupational health and safety training of workers and supervisors; its safeguards section says the root-cause analysis of both incidents pointed at gaps in site management and occupational health and safety practice, and the Bank's own supervision records had reported unsatisfactory performance on those points across the whole implementation period of the works component. After the deaths the incident reporting procedures were followed, the next of kin were compensated, a safety audit was carried out and regular on-site briefings were held. The completion report states that three workers died under circumstances that appear to have been preventable, and that site management and worker safety remained a perennial concern from the start of the works component, with the outcome proving unsatisfactory in Begusarai and Beur. On procurement, Bank guidelines were violated and misprocurement was declared on the Buxar sewage treatment plant and sewerage works, confidential information was leaked during the bid evaluation for the Munger sewage treatment plant and sewerage network, and preliminary bid evaluation reports prepared by implementing agencies were contested by the mission and the Bank and had to be revised. All three instances were in Bihar.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,103 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report counts 249 project-affected families at the Patna riverfront development, the only investment requiring full land acquisition, plus 20 households affected by partial land acquisition and 234 households affected by economic losses, and three people still to be compensated at the Digha site at closing.
card.outcome: The project closed on 30 December 2021 after a two-year extension, with US$466 million of the original US$1 billion commitment never used. All resettlement plans were recorded as implemented except one abbreviated plan covering three people at the Digha site. The Digha-Kankerbagh contract was carried forward to the Second National Ganga River Basin Project. The riverfront families received cash instead of the land they had been promised. The Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats the completion report's account of the three deaths and of the one outstanding plan, but does not mention the 249 families, the two-year delay in the land allotment, or the handing of sites to the contractor before people were resettled and paid; its summary says that all project-affected families were eventually compensated.
card.confidence_note: The 249 families, the two-year stall in the land allotment, the handing of sites to the contractor before people were resettled and paid, and the three deaths all come from the Bank's own completion report; the review of that report by the Independent Evaluation Group repeats the deaths and the single outstanding plan but not the rest. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of the Patna riverfront resettlement or of the two fatal incidents was found; a web search returned Indian press reports on other Ganga riverbank evictions and bridge projects in Bihar, none of them tied to this project. The three deaths are counted here because the report names a cause: its safeguards section gives gaps in site management and occupational health and safety practice and calls the circumstances apparently preventable, and its project-history annex gives negligence on occupational health and safety training of workers and supervisors. The same annex places one death at Begusarai in March 2021 and two at Beur in May 2021. The documents do not say who employed the dead. They name no affected family, do not say how many people the 249 families comprised, and do not say how much extra cash was paid in place of the promised land. The report also records that all the affected families were eventually compensated and trained for income restoration. The review carries no date anywhere on the page; the date used here is the Bank's own document date from its archive, unverified at document level.

card.whole: The riverfront works at Patna were the only such investment in the project: a promenade and pedestrian walkway connecting 16 ghats, which the completion report records as fully delivered. Across the project as a whole, by the report's count, 3.74 million people were direct beneficiaries, against a target of 3.57 million cut at the sixth restructuring in July 2021 from 4 million set at the fifth in October 2019, itself raised from 3.2 million; 17,450 tonnes a year of biochemical oxygen demand was abated against a target of 16,500 cut from the 21,000 set when that indicator was added in October 2019, which the report's table of target changes gives as 21,500; 404 million litres a day of untreated wastewater was kept out of the Ganga against a revised 386 and an appraisal 270; and 317,647 households were connected to sewerage against a target of 325,000, cut from the 475,310 set when that indicator too was added in October 2019, the report recording that no household-connection target existed at appraisal. The sewerage network built came to 2,632 kilometres against a revised target of 2,700 and the 3,570 set at the fifth restructuring. Five of six programme institutions were judged to be set up and working: the exception is the Bihar unit, where the report records over half the sanctioned posts vacant and poor performance in procurement, financial management and safeguards. Sixty real-time water quality monitoring stations were running against a revised target of 70. US$60.7 million was cancelled at the sixth restructuring, and the closing date was put back two years. The report puts the economic rate of return across the investments at 35.21 per cent with a benefit-cost ratio of 6.22 and a net present value of INR 140.80 billion at a 10 per cent discount rate, and for the Patna riverfront alone at 39.92 per cent, on costs of INR 206.39 crore against benefits of INR 1,908.26 crore; the appraisal document calculated no overall return because the investments had not been chosen, giving instead 13 to 32 per cent for generic sewage treatment plants. The Independent Evaluation Group rated efficiency Substantial and the outcome Satisfactory. The riverfront benefit figure rests in part on an estimate of increased economic activity made for the report, and every figure here is the lender's own; no independent check was found.
card.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered the policies on environmental assessment, involuntary resettlement, indigenous peoples, physical cultural resources, natural habitats and projects on international waterways. A resettlement policy and land acquisition framework was included in the environmental and social management framework and used throughout. Environmental management plans, social management plans and resettlement action plans for high-impact investments were prepared by third parties. The investment framework required priority to be given to land already under existing treatment plants or to government land transferred with a no-objection certificate, then to direct purchase, and only to compulsory acquisition where unavoidable; where it was used, resettlement plans and abbreviated plans were prepared and disclosed. The financing agreement was revised during implementation to include the provisions of India's Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013. The indigenous peoples policy was triggered by the presence of scheduled tribes, with the largest population in Jharkhand, where a dedicated consultation was held and a tribal management framework prepared; only Sahibganj district had a substantial tribal population and the investment there affected no tribal settlement. Under the international waterways policy China, Nepal and Bangladesh were notified and raised no objection. The physical cultural resources policy was triggered by possible effects of the riverfront development on cultural properties on the banks of the Ganga; the Patna environmental assessment identified religious sites that could be affected and the design was made to avoid them, so no management plan was required. A strategic environmental and social assessment was completed in March 2020 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 February 2023).

card.title: Second Karnataka State Highway Improvement: compensation paid into court, tax taken off payments
card.place: Karnataka state highways, including Malavalli-Pavagada, Mudhol-Nippani, Anandhapura-Shikaripura and Managili-Devapura, India

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-80220 for the Second Karnataka State Highway Improvement Project (P107649). US$350 million approved 24 March 2011, cut to US$295.2 million, all of which was disbursed. Closing was moved from 31 December 2016 to 28 December 2018. The completion report also lists trust fund TF-92428 (US$0.44 million original, US$0.18 million disbursed) and gives the project's effectiveness date as 17 July 2008 (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 23 October 2019).

lenders.name: Foreign private commercial sources (unidentified)
lenders.role: The Bank's completion report's financing table lists US$500 million at approval from 'Foreign Private Commercial Sources (unidentified)', revised to US$400 million, with US$416 million actually provided. The report does not name the lenders. The same report records US$416.56 million as the amount of new private sector capital the Government of Karnataka generated for improving and managing the state's core road network, which was one of the project's own outcome targets.

card.community: The Bank's completion report records 602 acres of private land taken from about 6,800 landowners, about 2,200 informal occupiers affected, and about 200 households physically displaced, of whom about 140 were informal occupiers. The independent evaluation the project commissioned at midterm in 2014 found living standards had risen on average, and also found that more than 90 per cent of affected people were not satisfied with the compensation amounts and that about 20 per cent had gone to court to get the amounts raised. The end-term evaluation in 2019, based on a survey of 700 affected families and a comparison group of 110 households, found a large proportion of compensation money, especially on the state highways side, had been paid into the courts because owners lacked ownership documents, and that 'these people faced several hardships in realizing the compensation amounts from the courts with high legal fees, long delays, multiple court hearings'. The same study found income tax had been deducted from compensation paid to people losing houses and structures in residential areas, which it says is against the resettlement policy adopted for the project; it names 7 landowners whose deductions were made by the state highways unit and 67 by the Karnataka Road Development Corporation, which the report says have to be repaid under the policy applied to the project. The completion report says over 40 per cent of compensation amounts were deposited with the courts, that the grievance committees were not functioning and that the database for tracking land acquisition and resettlement was not functioning. 1,235 complaints were made to the state highways unit and 543 to the road development corporation. In the 2019 survey about 15 per cent of affected people on the state highways side said their incomes were lower after resettlement, 52 per cent said they were the same and about a third said they had improved.
card.suppression: No arrests or police action are recorded. The completion report records 24 acres the corporation could not take possession of because landowners resisted until the courts released their compensation.
card.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the Bank's completion report or the Independent Evaluation Group review.
card.displaced_note: About 200 households physically displaced, about 140 of them informal occupiers, with about 6,800 landowners losing land and about 2,200 informal occupiers affected, per the World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report of 23 October 2019. ICIJ's 'Evicted and Abandoned' table gives 15,516, listed as an estimate of people displaced and taken from World Bank project documents as of 31 December 2014.
card.outcome: The Bank's rating for compliance with its resettlement policy, OP 4.12, stayed Unsatisfactory or Moderately Unsatisfactory for over three years, and the Bank and the state agreed remedial plans to bring the project back into compliance. The Independent Evaluation Group says 93 per cent of the land acquisition activities had been completed when the loan closed in December 2018. Outstanding in June 2019: compensation to 21 landowners not yet announced, resettlement assistance to 6 families, ownership titles for 27 families at the Hungsagi resettlement site in Yadgiri district, the resettlement of 31 displaced of Thangadagi village in Bijapur district, which the report does not say are people or families, 24 acres the corporation could not take possession of, and 6.23 acres of new land acquisition in 15 villages for drain improvements. The Bank rated the project's overall outcome Satisfactory and its own performance Satisfactory.
card.confidence_note: The core harm rests on the Bank's own documents alone: its completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report. The lender is reporting on its own project. The findings on compensation paid into court, on income tax deducted against the project's own resettlement policy, and on the two named villages are in the completion report, and the Independent Evaluation Group repeats them. The dissatisfaction and income figures come from two impact evaluations the project itself commissioned from consultants, in 2014 and 2019, not from independent field research. The same documents record rises in housing quality and asset ownership among resettled households, and both sets of findings are given here. No press report, court record or NGO field research on this project was found.

ICR Review: India - IN: Karnataka State Highway Improv Pro II (P107649)
Evicted and Abandoned: Second Karnataka State Highway Improvement (P107649)

card.whole: The Bank's completion report says the project financed capital improvement and maintenance works on 831 km of Karnataka's core road network. Its results table records 503 km completed under item-rate contracts against a revised target of 534 km, and 300 km under design-build-finance-operate-maintain-transfer concessions against a revised target of 301 km; 19 km was still unfinished at closing, 13 km held up by land acquisition and utility shifting and 6 km by works in progress. A further 1,078 km of non-rural roads were built as planned. It reports travel time on the project roads down 30 to 40 per cent against a target of 25 per cent, vehicle operating costs down 19 per cent against 15 per cent, and the share of the state's classified roads in good or fair condition up from 50 to 70 per cent, against a target the report's narrative gives as 65 per cent and its results table as 50 per cent. On the 62 km road safety demonstration corridor the report records deaths down 41 per cent against a target of 30 per cent and 143 accident blackspots treated in 2018-19; it gives the fall in accidents as 60 per cent in one passage and 66 per cent in another. The state raised US$416.56 million from private lenders against a revised target of US$400 million and an original target of US$500 million. Of that, the state road development corporation mobilised about US$97 million, which the report puts at about 60 per cent of the construction cost of the concession roads; the remaining 40 per cent was paid up front, in equal parts from the Bank loan and from a commercial bank. The project generated about 0.83 million days of unskilled work, 69 per cent of it going to local workers and 17 per cent to women. All these figures are the Bank's own. The report's economic rate of return was 32 per cent at completion against 30 per cent at appraisal, covering 97 per cent of project cost and built from vehicle operating cost savings, travel time savings and lower maintenance costs, and the Independent Evaluation Group, the Bank's internal evaluators, gave the same outcome, Bank performance and monitoring ratings as the report. No independent check was found.
card.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered OP/BP 4.12 on involuntary resettlement and OP/BP 4.11 on physical cultural resources. A resettlement policy framework and resettlement action plans were prepared and the policy was changed in 2014 to fit India's new land acquisition law. The project paid an extra 25 per cent compensation to landowners who agreed to the rates offered.
card.ecosystem: Trees were felled along the corridors. The completion report says 153,000 saplings were planted in compensatory planting against a plan of over 223,000, with the remaining 73,500 due by December 2019, and gives too few saplings, the rains and delays in finishing road stretches as the reasons. The project closed with a Satisfactory rating on environmental safeguard management.

card.title: Andhra Pradesh Forestry Projects and Podu Land Evictions
card.place: Tribal forest areas, Andhra Pradesh, India

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Financed the first-phase Andhra Pradesh Forestry Project (joint forest management, 1994 to 2000) and approved a US$108.2 million credit in 2002 for the Community Forest Management Project covering 3.86 million hectares of forest in 14 districts.

card.community: More than 15,000 hectares were taken over in the first phase. The NGO Samata (spelled Samatha in Down To Earth) says Adivasi (tribal) people were coerced into leaving forest land; the forest department says they left voluntarily (Down To Earth). In April 2002 the Bank agreed to cover tribal people evicted from podu (shifting cultivation) plots under its resettlement policy (Deccan Chronicle). In 2007 Samata and the Forest Peoples Programme found compensation inadequate and villagers asked to sign consent papers they did not understand; landless villagers displaced in the first phase were allegedly left out of benefits.
card.displaced_note: No count of evicted families is given; the Bank estimated 28% of people in project areas would be affected and prepared resettlement plans (Down To Earth).
card.outcome: A growing number of villages and local NGOs refused to carry out the resettlement plan and took grievances to the implementing agencies (Bretton Woods Project, 2007). Tribal people were already demanding the return of the vacated land in 2002 (Down To Earth).
card.confidence_note: The World Bank agreed in 2002 to cover tribal people evicted from podu plots under its resettlement policy and estimated 28% of people in project areas would be affected. The forest department says the land was given up voluntarily.

card.whole: The World Bank's evaluation office rated the first-phase project (a $77.4 million credit, closed 2000) 'highly satisfactory': about 850,000 hectares of degraded forest came under better management, more than twice the target, 2,666 village forest committees were formed, and dense forest cover in six sample districts rose about 19% from 1996. Sampled committee households gained about Rs 5,600 a year, but the studies missed losses such as less goat grazing; in the evaluators' own tribal survey 74% reported higher incomes, while everyone surveyed in villages without committees reported a fall. The same review rated the Bank's own performance unsatisfactory because forest encroachers were resettled in breach of its rules (OED, 2002). These are figures from the World Bank's own evaluation office; no independent check was found.
card.conditions: The 1994 project agreement for the first Andhra Pradesh Forestry Project (Credit 2573-IN) required the state to carry out an agreed Tribal Development Plan, run field investments under joint forest management plans with villagers, and adjust seedling prices every year to cover full production costs. The 2002 project agreement for the Community Forest Management Project (Credit 3692-IN) required Andhra Pradesh to comply with its Resettlement Action Plan and Tribal Development Plan, including village-level plans, and to set up an Independent Advisory Group to examine complaints about resettlement (World Bank, Project Agreements, 1994 and 2002).

card.title: Farmland taken and two households moved for Lesotho's road works
card.place: Nyenye to Makhoroana road, Leribe District, Lesotho

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Lesotho Integrated Transport Project (P075566), Credit IDA-42370 approved 19 October 2006, with later IDA-48270, grants IDA H-2550 and IDA H-6230 and trust fund TF-90728; the Financing Agreement for Credit 4827-LS and Grant H623-LS is dated 9 October 2010. The completion report of 21 December 2015 and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 27 June 2016 both rate the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The review rates the quality of supervision Moderately Unsatisfactory. The completion report rates safeguards performance moderately unsatisfactory.

companies.name: Ministry of Public Works and Transport, Lesotho
companies.role: Ran the project through a project implementation unit with posts for an environment and social coordinator, a resettlement desk and an HIV/AIDS coordinator. Both of the unit's safeguards specialists left in the project's second year and were not replaced for the additional financing, and no safeguards specialist joined the lender's own supervision missions for that stage.
companies.desc: A ministry of the government of Lesotho. The country's Roads Directorate began as a department inside it and was established as a separate corporate body by the Roads Directorate Act of 2010.

card.community: The credit paid for road works in Lesotho, including two bridges over the Senqu and Senqunyane rivers and work on two junction roads, Teyateyaneng to Mapoteng and Nyenye to Makhoroana. Floods in March 2011 damaged both roads so badly that the planned resealing had to become full rehabilitation; there was not enough credit for all 64 km, so the lender paid for the first 20 km of the Nyenye to Makhoroana road and the government undertook to cover the remaining 17 km and the Teyateyaneng to Mapoteng road. The completion report says the first assessment found resettlement "confined to two households", but that compensation also had to be paid for many strips of farmland where the road was widened for bus and taxi stops. When the additional financing was added, the report says, the assessment of its safeguards impacts was underestimated and implementation was unsatisfactory: environmental measures were neither systematically monitored nor documented, workers' safety measures "were only respected partially", and further resettlement activities were found later. New culverts, added when the road design changed, "induced adverse impacts on farmland", and the mission that wrote the report saw stones and loose material fallen onto the roads in many places. A small number of temporary market stalls were moved to make room for the works at Makhoroana. A new taxi rank was being built on land the local chief gave, and the report's authors objected that the taxi association had still not been formally engaged. No resettlement completion report was prepared. The Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats these findings and says that "it is not clear from the ICR whether the resettlement activities were complete at project closure". The report also records that prostitutes went to the construction camp, that condoms were often not available there because of its remote location, and that a social impacts study at completion found HIV infection rates had risen; the implementing agency denies that less attention was given to this under the additional financing.
card.killed_note: The completion report discusses road deaths in Lesotho as a policy problem, at around 15 deaths per 100,000 people a year, and records no death caused by the project's works.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 247 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report's only count of households resettled is two. It gives no number for the strips of farmland compensated, for the stalls moved, or for the resettlement activities found later.
card.outcome: The project closed in 2015. The completion report rates safeguards performance moderately unsatisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group says the report's account of safeguards compliance is unclear and that it cannot be told from it whether the project complied at closing. No resettlement completion report was produced, so there is no record of what the affected farmers were finally paid.
card.confidence_note: Everything here comes from the World Bank's completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it. The harm is real but small and poorly counted: two households resettled, an unnumbered set of farmland strips, and culverts that damaged farmland without any figure for the area or the farmers. No resettlement completion report exists, and the evaluation review says it cannot be told from the completion report whether the resettlement was finished. No Lesotho press report, court record or audit of these payments was found.

card.whole: The credit and its later financing rehabilitated roads and built footbridges in Lesotho. The completion report records 40 km of the Oxbow-Mokhotlong road rehabilitated against a revised target of 40 km, three footbridges and access tracks built in the Senqu and Senqunyane area, and the 37 km Nyenye-Makhoroana road substantially complete at closing and finished in December 2015, the first 20 km with Bank money and the remaining 17 km with government money. It gives average travel cost in the targeted project areas down 40 per cent to 900 maloti a trip, and national roads at 38 per cent good against a target of 39 per cent and 50 per cent fair against a target of 46 per cent. These figures are the lender's own; no independent check was found.
card.conditions: The conformed financing agreement of 21 November 2006 for Credit 4237-LS and Grant H255-LS required Lesotho, unless the Association agreed otherwise, to "carry out the Project, in accordance with the Environmental and Social Management Framework Plan" and not to amend, abrogate or waive that plan where the Association considered the change might materially or adversely affect the project (Schedule 2, Section I.C). The same schedule required Lesotho to establish a Roads Directorate within the Ministry of Public Works and Transport "no later than December 31, 2008", to "carry out the MPWT staff redeployment plan with due diligence and in accordance with timetables agreed upon with the Association", and to keep a project office staffed with, among others, an environmental and social coordinator (Section I.A.2 and I.A.3). The 2010 additional financing agreement for Credit 4827-LS and Grant H623-LS applied the original agreement's institutional arrangements to the new money and added only a requirement to update the project implementation manual, giving the Association the chance to review it first (Schedule 2, Sections I.A and I.B).
